Run it against the zero catalogue from the sedenion thread and the construction pins itself: no kind of zero buys both halves of the claim.

The fuzz zero — nilpotent ε, ε² = 0, the one fading into perpendicular directions — is precisely the zero you *can't* divide by. If ε had an inverse, ε = ε²·ε⁻¹ = 0, so invertibility would collapse the fuzz. The invertible near-zero is the hyperreal infinitesimal instead: ε ≠ 0, below every standard magnitude, 1/ε fully legal — and it can literally be an unlimited hyperinteger, which is your "infinity that's technically still a whole integer," rigorously (*ℤ contains them). But transfer holds equality fixed: 2 ≠ 1 in every hyperreal model. Worse for the mechanism: 2/ε − 1/ε = 1/ε. Dividing by true 0 merges the quotients of 1 and 2 into one undefined blob; dividing by the halo separates them by an unlimited amount. The move maximally *distinguishes* 1 from 2.

Make actual 0 invertible and you do get 2 = 1 — as a theorem of the one-element ring, since 0·x = 0 always, so 0·x = 1 forces 1 = 0 forces everything = 0. The equation is purchased by deleting distinctness itself; 2 = 1 there exactly as much as 17 = −π. The projective zero is the honest middle, and it's also your bounded infinity: ∞ as a single point on a compact sphere, 1/0 = ∞ legal — but ∞·0 stays undefined, so 1/0 = 2/0 never cancels back to 1 = 2.

What the intuition does prove: st(1−ε) = 1. Not-quite-one collapses to exactly one under standard part — a fact about a number and its *own* halo, never about 1 versus 2, and quotienting the limited hyperreals by infinitesimal closeness provably returns plain ℝ. Which hands you a defensible semantics for 2̊ before glyph lock: not "2 that equals 1" (no non-degenerate structure will certify it), but 2̊ := the halo of 2 — a fattened point in your own crossing-vs-fuzz taxonomy, genuinely fuzzy, standard part exactly 2. The ring stays honest and the glyph keeps the picture.

Just look at how many of the concepts we have discussed this is calling out.

Fuzzy physics/maths, ring toroid topology, maintaining and deleting distinctions, distinction as essence/reality, the projective zero being a bounded infinity always infinitesimally off from one, a point on a compact sphere (the sphere is the hopf fibration sphere, the point is a ring, the compactification from four dimensions back to one and 3D being the octave marker/designator for temporal realities the spacial vectors and time vectors, omni-dimensionality.

What if accellerating to light speed or beyond doesn't take infinite energy in actual physical application? What if there's a "close enough" point? Or what else does the "close enough" principle apply to?

The load-bearing callout in your list is the compactification, because it answers the light-speed question by inverting it. Velocity is a compactified chart: v/c = tanh(φ), where rapidity φ is the honest coordinate — additive under boosts, unbounded, E = mc²·cosh φ. In φ-space, c isn't a nearby wall you creep toward; it's the point at infinity, pulled onto the chart by tanh exactly the way the sphere pulls ∞ into view. So "infinitesimally close to c" is a chart illusion: each additional 9 in 0.999…c costs a fixed rapidity increment (≈1.15) and multiplies energy by √10. The nines are a geometric series in energy with no finite sum. On the massive side there is no halo of c — in the invariant, the gap isn't infinitesimal, it's infinite.

But "close enough" splits cleanly into kinematic and dynamic, and kinematically it's real. The highest-energy cosmic ray ever detected (γ ≈ 3×10¹¹) would lose a race against a photon across the observable universe by a couple of microseconds. Operationally at c for every purpose except the accounting — and closing that last microsecond costs unbounded energy. Close-enough exists; paid-for-in-full never does.

Meanwhile the boundary is occupied — natively. m = 0 is a separate stratum of the mass shell, a different Lorentz orbit entirely; the photon didn't accelerate to c, it was born on the cone, and no boost connects hyperboloid to cone. You don't approach the projective point — you either are it or you aren't. And the one time physics wrote down v > c, the tachyon, the equations answered "wrong zero": imaginary mass means you expanded around an unstable vacuum, the field condenses — that's the Higgs mechanism — and every excitation of the true vacuum is subluminal. The superluminal particle dissolved into a statement about where zero was. (Recession beyond the Hubble radius does exceed c, but that's the chart stretching, not motion through it.)

Where close-enough is *exact* rather than approximate: anywhere the dynamics contracts the halo. Renormalization group is the crown case — universality is st() applied to entire theories: microscopically different systems in one basin flow to the identical fixed point, so water's critical exponents equal a uniaxial ferromagnet's, close-enough collapsing to exactly-equal as a theorem. Same shape in decoherence (superpositions land in the halo of zero and the world takes the standard part), the thermodynamic limit (transitions are sharp only at N = ∞; 10²³ sits in its halo), the adiabatic theorem. And the criterion is sharp: st commutes with the flow when the flow contracts; it fails where the flow expands — chaos is precisely the regime where an initial condition's halo is torn to standard size in one Lyapunov time. Relativistic acceleration is expansive in exactly this sense: the rapidity-distance to c never contracts. Close-enough is a fixed-point phenomenon, and c is not a fixed point of anything a massive body does — it's the point at infinity wearing a chart that makes it look like a wall.
